lessons.title: Feudal England in 1189: Society, Towns and the Jewish Communities
lessons.description: Feudal hierarchy, peasant farming, towns, and the Jewish community on Richard I’s accession.
lessons.content_html:
When Richard I was crowned at Westminster on 3 September 1189, he inherited a kingdom of roughly 2.5 million people built on a steep social pyramid known as feudalism. The king sat at the top, holding all land in his own right; below him came tenants-in-chief (the great barons and bishops), then sub-tenants and knights, and at the base the unfree peasants who actually worked the soil. Land was the currency that bound it together. Those who held land owed service in return: armed knights for the king’s wars, days of labour for the lord’s fields, and a steady stream of cash payments at moments of family change.

Key Fact

England in 1189 was a feudal society of roughly 2.5 million people. The king granted land in return for knight service (military service) or labour service (work on the lord’s fields). Failure to perform service could lead to forfeiture — the loss of land back to the lord.

Homage, Knight Service and Forfeiture

A new tenant began his tenancy by performing homage. He knelt before his lord, placed his hands between the lord’s and swore to be his man. In return the lord granted him a fief — an estate of land. The grandest tenants, the tenants-in-chief, did homage directly to the king and owed him knight service: typically forty days’ armed service a year. Lower down the ladder, peasants performed labour service — ploughing, harvesting and carrying for the lord’s demesne (the home farm) on set days each week. If a tenant refused his service, rebelled, or committed a serious crime, his land could be taken back through forfeiture.

The Countryside: Peasant Life

More than nine in ten English people in 1189 lived in the countryside. The typical village was farmed under the open-field system: two or three great fields divided into long strips, with each peasant household holding scattered strips so that good and bad land was shared. Crops rotated each year — wheat or rye in one field, barley or oats in another, the third left fallow to recover. Common pasture, woodland and meadow were used by all. Most peasants were villeins (unfree), tied to the manor and unable to leave without the lord’s permission. They paid rent in labour (week-work and boon-work at harvest), in kind (eggs, hens, grain), and in cash. A small minority of free peasants held their land for money rent and could move on.

Life was hard. Famine followed bad harvests; a single wet summer could push a village to the edge. The lord’s manorial court enforced custom and punished offences. Yet the manor was also a community: the priest baptised, married and buried the villagers; the alewife brewed; the smith shod oxen. The peasant economy fed the kingdom and paid for the king’s wars.

Towns and the Economy

Towns were small by modern standards — London, the largest, had perhaps 25,000 people; York around 8,000 — but they were the engine of trade. A borough charter from the king or a great lord turned a market settlement into a self-governing borough, with the right to collect its own tolls, hold a regular market, and choose its own bailiffs. By 1189 around a hundred chartered towns dotted the kingdom. Wool was the great export — raw fleeces moved through Boston, Lincoln, York and London to Flemish and Italian buyers. Imports came back: wine from Gascony, cloth from Flanders, spices and silks through Venice. Towns also housed the craft guilds — weavers, tanners, bakers, fullers — whose ordinances set quality standards and trained apprentices.

Towns paid an annual sum called the farm of the borough straight into the royal exchequer. They were also a tax reserve: when Richard needed to raise his crusade or, later, his ransom, royal officers turned first to the wealthier boroughs and Jewish communities. Borough charters were therefore a two-way bargain — self-government in exchange for cash. The Cinque Ports of the south coast received special privileges in return for ship service to the Crown.

The Anglo-Jewish Community

A small Jewish community lived in around twenty English towns — principally London, York, Lincoln, Norwich, Lynn and Stamford — perhaps 5,000 people in total. They had been brought to England by William the Conqueror after 1066. Their legal status was distinctive: in law they belonged directly to the king as his property and were under his personal protection. This protection had a price. Jews could not own land or join most craft guilds, but they were permitted to lend money at interest, an activity the Church forbade Christians. They became the principal moneylenders to the Crown, the great barons and the higher clergy. Their loans helped finance castle-building, royal campaigns and the rebuilding of cathedrals at Norwich and St Albans.

Antisemitism was widespread, fuelled by religious hostility, the resentment of debtors, and lurid rumours such as the false ‘blood libel’ first circulated at Norwich in 1144. The Crown profited heavily from Jewish moneylending: Henry II had taxed the community at extraordinary rates, and Richard inherited that habit.

Key Fact

The pogroms of 1189–90 began at Richard I’s coronation banquet on 3 September 1189 and reached their worst point at York’s Clifford’s Tower on 16 March 1190. Around 150 Jews died there. Indebted Norman gentry led by Richard Malebisse then burned the moneylending records held in the cathedral.

The Pogroms of 1189–90

Richard’s coronation triggered the worst antisemitic violence in English history to that point. A delegation of Jewish leaders arrived at Westminster Hall to present gifts; they were refused entry, beaten, and rumours spread through the city that the king had ordered an attack. A London mob burned Jewish homes and killed those they found. Over the winter of 1189–90 the violence travelled north — Norwich, Lynn, Stamford, Lincoln — reaching its climax at York on 16 March 1190, when around 150 Jews who had taken refuge in Clifford’s Tower were killed or chose to take their own lives rather than be murdered.

Students often write that the 1189–90 attacks were spontaneous bigotry. English Heritage research on Clifford’s Tower shows otherwise. The York massacre was led by indebted Norman gentry — particularly Richard Malebisse — who immediately afterwards rode to York Minster and burned the bonds (the written debt records) that were stored there. Wiping out the moneylenders also wiped out their debts. Antisemitic feeling around Richard’s coronation and crusading fervour gave the violence its religious cover, but the engine was debt politics.

After the violence Richard was furious — not because Jews had died, but because his property had been destroyed. The king ordered an inquiry, fined some of the rioters and set up the archae, chests in which fresh copies of every loan would be kept under royal oversight. The Crown’s grip on the Jewish community tightened, and royal exploitation through tallages (special taxes) intensified through the 1190s.

Do not blur the two into a single paragraph; the mark scheme rewards clear separation. Use precise medieval vocabulary (homage, fief, villein, demesne, pogrom, tallage) for top-band SPaG.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Feudal England in 1189 was a hierarchy of landholders bound by homage, knight service and labour service, with forfeiture as the penalty for failure to serve.
  • Most people were unfree peasants farming the open fields under the manor; a hundred chartered towns and the wool trade provided the king with crucial revenue.
  • The Anglo-Jewish community lived under direct royal protection as moneylenders — the 1189–90 pogroms, climaxing at Clifford’s Tower on 16 March 1190, were driven as much by debt politics as by religious hatred.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the feudal hierarchy in England in 1189.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for a valid identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• The king as ultimate landlord — all land in England was held from the king; tenants-in-chief did homage directly to him.
• Knight service — tenants-in-chief owed roughly forty days of armed military service a year in return for their fief.
• Labour service — villeins worked the lord’s demesne for set days each week (week-work) and extra days at harvest (boon-work).
• Homage — the kneeling oath ceremony in which a tenant placed his hands between his lord’s and swore loyalty in return for land.
• Forfeiture — the legal seizure of a tenant’s land if he rebelled, refused service, or committed a serious crime.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail; one may be more developed than the other.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or generic.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Anglo-Jewish community was so important to royal finances in 1189.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Christian ban on usury
• royal protection of Jews
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Christian ban on usury — Church doctrine forbade Christians from lending at interest, leaving Jewish lenders as the principal source of credit for barons, bishops and the Crown.
• Direct royal protection — Jews were legally the king’s property under his personal protection, meaning the wealth they accumulated was effectively a Crown reserve to be tapped through tallages.
• Concentration in towns — communities clustered in around twenty boroughs including London, York, Lincoln, Norwich and Lynn, putting their wealth within easy reach of royal officers.
• Restrictions on alternative occupations — bans on landholding and most craft guilds channelled Jewish economic activity into finance and trade, the very sectors that produced taxable cash wealth.
• Loans for royal projects — Jewish credit funded castle-building, royal campaigns and the rebuilding of cathedrals at Norwich and St Albans, all of which served Crown interests.
• Extraordinary tallages — Henry II had taxed the community at extraordinary rates and Richard inherited the habit; tallages produced large lump sums quickly without parliamentary or baronial consent.
• The archae system — after the 1189–90 pogroms, royal chests holding fresh copies of every loan ensured the Crown could always estimate, and tax, the community’s wealth.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence and clear weighting; both stimulus points developed; own information adds substance beyond the prompts.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation and supporting detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy; some narrative.
Emerging: Limited reasons; explanation thin or descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Jewish communities of England suffered violent attacks in 1189–90.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Richard I’s coronation
• the role of indebted Norman gentry
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explanation of distinct, supported reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• Richard’s coronation on 3 September 1189 — a Jewish delegation bringing gifts to Westminster was refused entry and beaten; rumours that the king had sanctioned an attack triggered a London mob to burn Jewish homes that night.
• Indebted Norman gentry — the York massacre at Clifford’s Tower on 16 March 1190 was led by Richard Malebisse and other gentry; immediately afterwards they rode to York Minster and burned the moneylending bonds, wiping out their own debts.
• Crusading fervour — Richard had taken the Cross; preachers framed the upcoming Third Crusade as a war against the enemies of Christ, and crowds extended that hatred to local Jewish communities.
• Religious antisemitism — long-standing prejudices, including the false ‘blood libel’ circulated at Norwich in 1144, made Jewish communities easy targets.
• Royal exploitation — heavy tallages had pushed barons and gentry to borrow from Jewish lenders, breeding resentment that erupted when royal protection seemed weakened by Richard’s departure plans.

Mastering: Three or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative of events with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why labour service mattered so much to lords on a typical English manor in 1189.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the lord’s demesne
• the open-field system
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• The lord’s demesne — the home farm produced the food and wool that fed the lord’s household and generated cash; without villein labour it could not be ploughed, sown or harvested on time.
• The open-field system — ploughing, sowing and harvesting had to happen across great fields in narrow seasonal windows; week-work and boon-work concentrated peasant labour at exactly those moments.
• Cash-poor manors — coin was scarce in rural England; paying free wage labourers would have been impossible for most lords, so the customary obligation to work was the only way to get it done.
• Social control — labour service tied villeins to the manor and to the lord’s court, reinforcing the authority of the manorial system.
• Surplus for sale — what the demesne produced beyond the household’s needs went to market in nearby boroughs, providing the lord with cash for taxes, ransoms and royal service.

Mastering: Three or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation; both stimulus points developed and own information added.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
‘Religious hatred was the main reason for the pogroms of 1189–90.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Third Crusade
• debts owed to Jewish moneylenders
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Richard had taken the Cross; the Third Crusade was preached as a war against the enemies of Christ and crowds extended that hatred to local Jewish communities.
• The false ‘blood libel’ first circulated at Norwich in 1144 was repeated by preachers, casting Jewish neighbours as ritual murderers.
• The trigger event was the coronation banquet at Westminster, where Jewish leaders bringing gifts were refused entry on grounds that they could not approach the Christian rite.
• Religious feeling allowed mobs in London, Norwich, Lynn, Stamford and Lincoln to act with a sense of righteousness rather than guilt.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Debts owed to Jewish moneylenders — the York massacre was led by indebted Norman gentry under Richard Malebisse who burned the bonds at York Minster immediately afterwards, wiping out their debts.
• Royal absence — Richard was preparing to leave for the Holy Land; ringleaders calculated that royal protection would be weakened and prosecution unlikely.
• Royal exploitation — Henry II’s and Richard’s heavy tallages had forced Jewish lenders to call in loans aggressively, breeding resentment that turned violent at the first opportunity.
• Local crowd dynamics — once the London violence began, rumour and copying spread the pattern north along trading routes through the winter of 1189–90.

Overall judgement: Religious hostility provided the cover and the language, but the engine of the worst violence at York was debt politics and the calculation by indebted gentry that royal absence would shield them; without those material motives the killings would not have escalated as they did. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly and reach a justified conclusion using precise period vocabulary (pogrom, tallage, bonds, Crusade).

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

lessons.title: Kingship, Succession and Ruling England in Richard's Absence
lessons.description: Angevin kingship, Richard’s claim, and Hubert Walter’s government 1189–99.
lessons.content_html:
When Henry II died in July 1189, the throne passed to his eldest surviving son Richard. Medieval English kingship was not a job description but a sacred office. The king was crowned and anointed by the Archbishop of Canterbury at Westminster, marking him out as God’s representative on earth. He was expected to keep the peace, defend the kingdom, dispense justice through his courts, and lead his army in war. He was also expected to take the advice of his Curia Regis (the king’s council of great barons and bishops). In return he held immense power: he summoned and dismissed assemblies, granted charters, levied taxes, and could pardon or condemn anyone in his realm.

The Role of the Church

The Church shaped kingship at every level. The coronation rite at Westminster — oath, anointing, crown, sceptre — framed Richard as a sacred figure rather than merely a powerful one. Bishops sat on the king’s council and ran much of his administration; the Archbishop of Canterbury was the second person in the realm. The Church also gave the king a vast pool of literate, trained men. Most senior administrators (justiciars, chancellors, treasurers, sheriffs’ clerks) held Church offices that funded their service to the Crown without costing the royal exchequer a salary. The price of this convenience was that bishops answered to two masters: the king who appointed them and the Pope in Rome.

Key Fact

A medieval English king was expected to keep the peace, dispense justice and defend the kingdom in war. The coronation rite — oath, anointing with holy oil, crowning by the Archbishop of Canterbury — turned a prince into God’s appointed ruler.

Richard’s Claim and Coronation

Richard’s claim to the throne in 1189 was strong but not unchallenged. He was the eldest surviving son of Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine; his elder brothers Henry the Young King and Geoffrey were already dead. He had spent the last years of his father’s reign in armed rebellion alongside his brothers, but the deathbed reconciliation at Chinon left him as the obvious heir. The other claimant was Geoffrey’s young son Arthur of Brittany — Richard’s nephew — whose case rested on the rule that a dead son’s line should inherit. The English barons accepted Richard. He was crowned at Westminster on 3 September 1189 in a sumptuous ceremony designed to broadcast continuity and legitimacy across the Angevin world.

Securing power required money. Richard had taken the Cross before his father’s death and intended to leave on crusade within months. To raise funds he sold offices, charters and even castles — he is supposed to have joked that he would sell London if he could find a buyer. Sheriffs purchased their counties; barons purchased confirmations of their lands. The king then levied a special tax called the Saladin Tithe his father had begun, set up his administration and sailed for the Holy Land in summer 1190.

Richard’s Character

Contemporaries called Richard ‘Coeur de Lion’ — Lionheart — for his bravery and military skill. He was tall, charismatic, fluent in French and Occitan (his court language as Duke of Aquitaine), and a trained warrior who had been crushing rebellious vassals in Aquitaine since his teens. He was also impatient, hot-tempered, and, by modern standards, almost wholly absent from England: in his ten-year reign he spent only about six months in his English kingdom. To Richard, England was a quarry — a rich source of revenue and recruits for war elsewhere, especially in defence of his far larger French lands. The Angevin Empire stretched from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees, and Richard cared most about its French heartlands.

Many students arrive thinking Richard was a heroic English king and John a villain — the legacy of the Robin Hood story. The reality is more complicated. Richard spent only about six months of his reign in England and drained the country with crusade taxes and his ransom; John, by contrast, was almost continuously present and ran a tight, intrusive administration. The popular contrast is largely a creation of later legend. Modern historians (W.L. Warren onwards) stress that Richard’s reputation rests on his battlefield reputation, not on his record as a ruler of England.

Governing England 1189–99: Hubert Walter

A king who lived abroad needed deputies who could rule in his name. Richard’s first attempt — co-justiciars William de Mandeville and Hugh du Puiset, soon replaced by the unpopular William Longchamp — ended in chaos when his brother John tried to seize control during 1191. Returning from the Holy Land in 1193, Richard appointed Hubert Walter as Archbishop of Canterbury and chief justiciar. Walter became, in effect, the working head of government. He chaired the Curia Regis, ran the Exchequer, supervised the courts and oversaw the network of sheriffs.

Walter’s greatest achievement was raising the king’s ransom of 100,000 marks (later increased to 150,000) after Richard’s capture in Austria. He levied a tax of one-quarter on income and moveables, took church plate, sequestrated the wool clip of the Cistercian monasteries, and squeezed the Jewish community through extraordinary tallages. He also reformed the administration of justice: itinerant justices toured the shires every few years, hearing pleas of the Crown and standardising the king’s law. The 1194 Articles of Eyre laid down what they should ask. Coroners were introduced in 1194 to record sudden deaths and royal pleas, freeing the sheriffs for revenue work and creating a check on local corruption.

Key Fact

From 1193, Hubert Walter ran England as Archbishop of Canterbury and chief justiciar. He raised Richard’s ransom of 150,000 marks, reformed the eyre system of justice, and created the office of coroner in 1194 to record royal pleas in each county.

Sheriffs, the Exchequer and the Royal Demesne

The shire-by-shire backbone of English government was the sheriff. The sheriff collected royal revenues from the king’s lands, courts, fines and feudal dues, banked them at the twice-yearly Exchequer at Westminster (with copies of the accounts kept on rolls of parchment called pipe rolls), presided over the shire court, and led the county levy in arms. He was a powerful, often resented figure; sheriffs typically bought their counties at a stiff price and made it back over the term of office. The royal demesne — lands held directly by the Crown rather than granted to tenants — provided a substantial income that did not depend on parliamentary or baronial consent.

Several factors held the system together. First, the institutions were already strong: Henry II had built a professional Exchequer, a network of itinerant royal justices, and a chain of sheriffs who reported twice a year. Second, Hubert Walter was an outstanding administrator who could chair the Curia Regis, run finance and supervise the courts simultaneously. Third, Eleanor of Aquitaine acted as senior queen-mother and political fixer. Fourth, John’s 1191–94 attempt to seize power gave the loyal barons a clear enemy and pushed them to defend Richard’s government. Fifth, the Pope and the Archbishop of Canterbury anchored Richard’s legitimacy even from Westminster. Together these meant that England paid its taxes, raised its ransom and held its peace through a decade of royal absence.

By the end of Richard’s reign in 1199, England was financially exhausted but administratively more sophisticated than when he had started. The Crown had a written record of its revenues, a regular eyre, a coroner system, and a chief minister who had absorbed the daily burden of government. These were the tools that John would inherit — and that he would test to breaking point.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Why question on government in Richard’s absence, identify three distinct reasons (institutions, Hubert Walter, John’s rebellion forcing baronial loyalty), give precise period detail (Exchequer, eyre, coroners 1194, ransom of 150,000 marks) and keep your focus on causation rather than narrative. Avoid the temptation to retell the crusade story; the question is about how England was held together at home.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Medieval kingship combined sacred ritual (the Westminster coronation and anointing) with practical duties of justice, defence and revenue, with the Church providing both legitimacy and a pool of trained administrators.
  • Richard’s claim was strong (eldest surviving son of Henry II) but his interests lay in war and the French heartlands of the Angevin Empire; he spent only about six months of his reign in England.
  • From 1193, Hubert Walter as Archbishop and chief justiciar held the kingdom together — raising the king’s ransom, reforming the eyre, and introducing coroners in 1194 — using the strong institutions Henry II had built.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of how Richard I secured his power in 1189.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Coronation at Westminster — on 3 September 1189 he was anointed and crowned by the Archbishop, broadcasting legitimacy across the Angevin Empire.
• Sale of offices and charters — he sold sheriffdoms, confirmed baronial charters for cash, and was said to have joked that he would sell London if he could.
• Continuation of the Saladin Tithe — the 10% tax begun by Henry II to fund the crusade, swelling royal coffers.
• Reconciliation with John — he granted his brother extensive lands and a generous income to keep him quiet while away.
• Appointment of trusted ministers — chancellor William Longchamp, justiciars and bishops to govern in his name.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Hubert Walter was such an effective head of government for England 1193–98.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the offices he held
• his reforms of justice
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Combined offices — as Archbishop of Canterbury and chief justiciar he commanded both the moral authority of the senior English see and the secular authority to chair the Curia Regis, run the Exchequer and supervise the courts.
• Reforms of justice — the 1194 Articles of Eyre standardised what royal justices asked when they toured the shires, and the introduction of county coroners in 1194 created a check on the sheriffs.
• Raising the ransom — he extracted 150,000 marks of silver in 1193–94 through a quarter tax on income and moveables, the Cistercian wool clip, church plate and tallages on the Jewish community, holding the Crown’s credit at its weakest moment.
• Continuity with Henry II’s institutions — he ran a system already strong (Exchequer, eyre, sheriffs, pipe rolls), enabling effective government in the king’s absence.
• Royal trust — Richard knew Walter from the crusade and trusted him with the Great Seal; this confidence allowed bold policy decisions without fear of repudiation.
• Defeat of John’s 1191–94 coup — Walter (with Eleanor) co-ordinated the loyalist response, recovering John’s castles at Marlborough and Lancaster.
• Diplomatic reach — as Archbishop he could correspond with the Pope and negotiate with foreign powers, providing tools no lay justiciar could match.

Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation and supporting detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy; some narrative.
Emerging: Limited reasons; explanation thin or descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why royal government in England did not collapse during Richard I’s long absence on crusade.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Hubert Walter
• the Exchequer
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explanation of distinct, supported reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• Hubert Walter as chief justiciar — from 1193 he chaired the Curia Regis, ran the Exchequer and supervised the courts, providing a single, capable head of government able to make decisions in the king’s name.
• The Exchequer — Henry II’s twice-yearly accounting system, with sheriffs reporting and pipe rolls recording revenue, kept the Crown’s finances functional even when the king was overseas.
• The eyre and the sheriffs — itinerant royal justices and county sheriffs delivered justice and collected revenue in a regular pattern that did not depend on the king’s personal presence.
• Eleanor of Aquitaine — the queen-mother acted as a political fixer, holding the great barons together and helping to negotiate her son’s release.
• John’s rebellion — his attempt to seize power in 1191–94 gave loyal barons a clear enemy and rallied them around the legitimate government.
• The Church — the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Pope reaffirmed Richard’s legitimacy, deterring serious challengers from open revolt.

Mastering: Three or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Church played such a central role in royal government in 1189.
You may use the following in your answer:
• coronation
• literate clerks and bishops
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• Coronation legitimacy — the anointing by the Archbishop of Canterbury made the king God’s appointed ruler, sanctifying his authority over the laity.
• Literate administrators — in an age when most laymen could not read Latin, bishops and clerks staffed the Exchequer, courts and chancery.
• Free pool of officials — clerks held Church benefices that paid them a salary, so the Crown got skilled administrators without bleeding its own treasury.
• Bishops on the Curia Regis — senior churchmen sat alongside the great barons in the king’s council, advising on policy.
• Diplomatic links — bishops carried letters between courts and to Rome, providing a working diplomatic network that lay barons could not match.
• Spiritual sanctions — excommunication and interdict were powerful weapons that bound the Church into political crises (a fact John would discover in 1208).

Mastering: Three or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation; both stimulus points developed and own information added.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
‘Hubert Walter was the main reason England held together while Richard was absent.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the ransom of 1194
• the strength of Henry II’s institutions
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Hubert Walter ran the Curia Regis, the Exchequer and the courts simultaneously, providing a single head of government able to make decisions in the king’s name.
• He raised the king’s ransom of 150,000 marks in 1193–94 through a quarter tax, the Cistercian wool clip and church plate, holding the Crown’s credit together at its weakest moment.
• He reformed the eyre and introduced coroners in 1194, strengthening institutions even while the king was away.
• As Archbishop of Canterbury he commanded the moral authority needed to keep the great barons in line.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Henry II’s institutions — the Exchequer, pipe rolls, professional sheriffs and itinerant justices were already in place by 1189; Walter ran a system he had inherited.
• Eleanor of Aquitaine — the queen-mother held the political coalition together and was central to the ransom negotiations and to defeating John in 1194.
• John’s rebellion — the very threat of his coup in 1191–94 united the loyal barons behind the legitimate government.
• Papal and ecclesiastical pressure — the Pope and bishops reinforced Richard’s legitimacy and discouraged open revolt.
• Royal absence as a stabiliser — with the king on crusade, baronial factions had little to gain by toppling a government whose most popular figure (Walter) was running things competently.

Overall judgement: Hubert Walter was indispensable, but he succeeded because he was running Henry II’s machinery, with Eleanor of Aquitaine and the Church reinforcing legitimacy and John’s rebellion clarifying loyalties. A balanced judgement weighs Walter’s talent against the institutional inheritance and political support he could draw on.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout (justiciar, eyre, ransom, archae, demesne).
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

lessons.title: The Third Crusade: Causes, Acre and Arsuf
lessons.description: Fall of Jerusalem 1187, why English crusaders went, and Richard’s victories at Acre and Arsuf.
lessons.content_html:
A crusade was a holy war called by the Pope and waged by Christians for spiritual reward. The First Crusade had captured Jerusalem in 1099 and established a string of Latin Christian states along the eastern Mediterranean. By the 1180s those states were under enormous pressure from a unified Muslim power based in Egypt and Syria under Saladin. On 4 July 1187 Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at the Battle of Hattin, capturing the True Cross and the king. Within months Acre, Sidon, Beirut and other cities had fallen. On 2 October 1187 Saladin entered Jerusalem itself. The shock in Western Europe was immense.

Key Fact

Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187 and entered Jerusalem on 2 October 1187. The fall of the Holy City triggered Pope Gregory VIII’s call for a Third Crusade in his bull Audita tremendi.

Crusading Attitudes in England

When the news from the Holy Land reached England, attitudes were shaped by a century of crusading culture. Sermons in parish churches told stories of First Crusade heroes; the great religious orders (Templars and Hospitallers) had houses across the country; pilgrimage badges from Jerusalem were valued relics. Pope Gregory VIII’s 1187 bull Audita tremendi framed the loss of Jerusalem as a punishment for Christian sin and called for armed pilgrimage. Anyone who took the Cross gained an indulgence — the remission of the punishment for their sins — and protection of their lands and debts while away. Henry II and Philip II of France immediately took the Cross at Gisors on 21 January 1188. Richard, then count of Poitou, took it later that year. He was the first ruler in north-western Europe to swear the crusading vow. He never took it back.

The English Crusading Army

Who actually went on crusade from England? The army that left in 1190 was a cross-section of Angevin society, not just the king and his knights. Tenants-in-chief took the Cross with their household knights; bishops — including the Archbishop of Canterbury, Baldwin of Forde — led contingents from their dioceses. Below them came mounted sergeants (men-at-arms without the full knightly equipment), foot soldiers raised from the shires, archers, crossbowmen, and a large body of non-combatants — cooks, smiths, surgeons, clerks, and pilgrims of every social rank. A separate seaborne contingent from the Cinque Ports, London and the East Anglian harbours sailed on around a hundred ships, picked up further crusaders en route in Lisbon (where they helped storm a small Moorish fortress at Silves in 1189), and met the king in Sicily. Total English numbers were perhaps 8,000 fighting men and several thousand non-combatants.

Why did they go? Motives were mixed. Many were genuinely moved by the loss of Jerusalem and the chance of an indulgence; some hoped for booty and lands in the East; some came to escape debts or law-suits; some were summoned by feudal duty to a lord who had taken the Cross. The crusader vow gave each one a moral and legal status that bound them all together for the journey.

Students sometimes assume that crusaders went East purely for plunder. The financial reality argues against this: crusade was breathtakingly expensive. A knight had to provide his armour, three or four horses, supplies for a campaign of years, and probably had to mortgage land or borrow heavily to do it. Many came home poorer than they left. The indulgence and the religious framing mattered. The 1188 Saladin Tithe and the 1193–94 ransom both show how seriously the wealthy laity were prepared to pay for the cause. Profit was a hope; piety was the engine.

Richard’s Motives

Richard had personal as well as political reasons to go. As Duke of Aquitaine and a man raised on the chivalric culture of southern France, he had grown up on stories of Roland and the First Crusade. The fall of Jerusalem stirred a genuine religious response. But there were also kingly calculations. The crusade was the most prestigious enterprise a Christian ruler could undertake; success would set him above every other monarch in Europe. He had taken the Cross before becoming king, and to renege after his coronation would have damaged his reputation across Christendom. Practically, the crusade also gave him a cause around which to organise the Angevin Empire and to extract enormous taxes from England and his French lands.

Quarrels with Philip II

From the start the Third Crusade was a fragile alliance. Richard and Philip II of France had been allies as princes against Henry II, but as kings they were rivals for the great Angevin lands in France. They wintered together in Sicily in 1190–91, where their tempers frayed: Richard repudiated his betrothal to Philip’s sister Alys (alleging she had been Henry II’s mistress), seized Messina from its Norman ruler, and married Berengaria of Navarre instead. He then conquered Cyprus from its Byzantine renegade lord Isaac Komnenos in May 1191. Philip arrived at Acre first; Richard joined him in June. Both contributed to the siege, but the personal hostility between the two kings was barely concealed and it would shape the strategic disaster of the next year.

The Siege and Capture of Acre, 1191

Acre was the great port and economic capital of the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem. King Guy of Lusignan had been besieging it since 1189 with a small force; the besieging Christians were themselves besieged in turn by Saladin’s field army. The arrival of Philip II’s contingent in spring 1191 and Richard’s in June transformed the operation. Richard brought up siege engines, mantlets and trebuchets — including a giant trebuchet known as the ‘Bad Neighbour’. Mining undermined the towers. After heavy losses on both sides Acre’s garrison surrendered on 12 July 1191. The terms included the return of the True Cross, the release of 1,500 Christian prisoners, and a ransom of 200,000 dinars. When Saladin delayed payment Richard ordered the execution of around 2,700 Muslim prisoners outside the city walls in late August — a decision still debated by historians and a permanent stain on his reputation. Philip II, citing illness, sailed home shortly afterwards.

Key Fact

Acre fell on 12 July 1191 after a two-year siege. Two months later Richard defeated Saladin at the Battle of Arsuf on 7 September 1191. Saladin lost around 7,000 men; Richard lost around 700.

The March to Jaffa and the Battle of Arsuf

Richard now needed to secure the coast as a supply route before any move on Jerusalem. He marched south from Acre towards Jaffa in late August 1191, hugging the coastline so that his fleet could shadow him with food and water. Saladin shadowed him inland with mounted archers, harassing the column day after day. Richard kept tight discipline: knights did not break ranks despite the provocation, crossbowmen replied from within the marching column, and the army moved in three solid blocks — van, centre, rear — with the baggage shielded between army and sea.

On 7 September the column reached the wood of Arsuf and Saladin attacked in force, hoping to break the rear of the column under the Hospitallers. The Hospitallers held until they could hold no longer; their charge, joined moments later by the rest of the line, broke the Muslim army. Saladin lost around 7,000 men, Richard about 700. The victory at Arsuf restored the prestige of the Christian arms after Hattin and proved that a disciplined western army could survive in the field against Saladin. It opened the road to Jaffa, which Richard took and refortified.

Acre was the gateway to the Holy Land — without it no large crusader army could be supplied. Its fall in July 1191 reopened the supply line to Europe and gave the crusaders a base from which to march on Jerusalem. Arsuf showed that Saladin’s field army was not invincible. Together the two victories built the legend of Richard the Lionheart in Christendom and reset the strategic position. They could not, however, replace the loss of Christian numbers, of Philip’s troops, and of the political will to take Jerusalem itself — problems that Lesson 4 will examine.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Describe Two Features question on the English crusading army or the causes of the crusade, give two genuinely different features — for example one about composition (knights, sergeants, foot, fleet) and one about motivation (indulgence, feudal duty, religious response to Hattin) — with one supporting detail each. Use precise period vocabulary (indulgence, taking the Cross, Audita tremendi, Saladin Tithe) for top-band SPaG. Do not drift into a narrative of the campaign; that belongs in 8 and 16-mark questions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Saladin’s victory at Hattin and capture of Jerusalem in 1187 triggered the Third Crusade; Audita tremendi framed it as armed pilgrimage with an indulgence for those who took the Cross.
  • The English crusading army of 1190 was a cross-section of Angevin society — tenants-in-chief, bishops, sergeants, foot, archers, fleet and pilgrims — with mixed religious, financial and feudal motives.
  • Acre fell on 12 July 1191 after a two-year siege, and Richard’s victory at Arsuf on 7 September 1191 restored the prestige of Christian arms but did not yet recapture Jerusalem.

lessons.title: Jerusalem Lost, Ransom Paid: Richard's Return and Capture
lessons.description: Why Richard could not retake Jerusalem, his capture, and the ransom that drained England.
lessons.content_html:
After the victories at Acre and Arsuf in summer 1191 the road to Jerusalem seemed open. Richard refortified Jaffa and pushed inland twice in late 1191 and early 1192 — up the road to Beit Nuba, only twelve miles from the Holy City. Both times he turned back. The failure to recapture Jerusalem was not the failure of one battle but of an entire strategic position. Several factors closed in on the king at the same time.

The Logistical Problem

Jerusalem sat in arid hill country some forty miles from the coast. Even if the crusaders captured it, the city would have to be supplied by mule trains across that distance, through territory dotted with Muslim castles. Saladin had already destroyed walls and water cisterns in towns along the route to deny their use to the crusaders. Richard’s council of war — particularly the local barons of the surviving Latin kingdom — argued that even a successful assault on Jerusalem would be undone the next campaigning season as soon as the bulk of the western army went home and Saladin counter-attacked the long supply line. Richard accepted the argument with reluctance. He is supposed to have refused to look at Jerusalem from a distance, saying that he was unworthy to see what he could not conquer.

Key Fact

Philip II of France sailed home in August 1191 shortly after Acre fell. Once back in France, he intrigued with John against Richard’s lands, putting permanent pressure on Richard to come home before he could finish the crusade.

Philip II’s Departure and the Threat to Normandy

Soon after Acre fell, Philip II announced he was ill and sailed home in August 1191. The departure of the French king was a strategic disaster for Richard. It removed a substantial part of the army; it allowed Philip to plot against Richard’s lands in France while Richard himself was thousands of miles away; and it took with it the political legitimacy of a joint royal crusade. By spring 1192 Richard was hearing that John, in concert with Philip, was attempting to seize the Angevin Empire and make himself effective king of England. Every week Richard stayed in the Holy Land was a week that his French inheritance bled. The clock that drove him home had started ticking the moment Philip raised sail.

Internal Christian Division and Saladin’s Strategy

The Christian camp was split. Conrad of Montferrat and the local barons of the Latin Kingdom wanted Conrad as king of Jerusalem; Richard backed Guy of Lusignan. The dispute was only resolved with Conrad’s assassination by the Order of Assassins on 28 April 1192 (a killing rumour blamed, probably unfairly, on Richard) and the elevation of Henry II of Champagne. Even then Christian command was fragile, with Pisans, Genoese, Templars, Hospitallers, French and English barons all pulling in different directions.

Saladin, meanwhile, played a careful game. He was not strong enough to drive Richard out of Acre and Jaffa, but he did not have to be. Wherever Richard pushed, Saladin destroyed wells and cisterns, kept his field army intact, and waited. He understood that Richard’s political problems in France would force the king to compromise. The two sides agreed the Treaty of Jaffa on 2 September 1192. Jerusalem stayed in Muslim hands; the Christians kept Acre, Jaffa and the coastal strip; unarmed Christian pilgrims were guaranteed access to the Holy Sepulchre. Richard sailed for home a month later.

Students sometimes argue that the Third Crusade was a Christian success because Richard took Acre, won at Arsuf and signed the Treaty of Jaffa. The strategic test, though, is whether the crusade achieved its stated aim — the recovery of Jerusalem. It did not. The Treaty of Jaffa kept the Holy City in Muslim hands; the crusader states were reduced to a coastal strip; and Richard’s reputation as ‘Lionheart’ was built on tactical military skill rather than strategic crusading success. The campaign ended not with Richard riding into Jerusalem but with him in chains in an Austrian castle. Top-band answers acknowledge his battlefield achievement while explaining why the crusade failed against the criterion the Pope had set in 1187.

Richard’s Return and Capture

Richard left the Holy Land in October 1192. He could not sail north up the western Mediterranean because Philip II controlled the southern French coast and would have arrested him; Spanish coasts were closed by political agreements; the route through Italy was unsafe because of his quarrel with the German emperor Henry VI. He chose to sail north and slip overland through the lands of his enemies. A storm wrecked his ship in the Adriatic in December 1192. Travelling in disguise he was recognised near Vienna and seized by Duke Leopold V of Austria, whose banner Richard had thrown into the moat at Acre. Leopold handed Richard over to Henry VI in March 1193. The Holy Roman Emperor demanded a ransom of 100,000 marks of silver, soon raised to 150,000 — an extraordinary sum equal to two or three years of total English royal revenue.

Key Fact

Richard was captured by Duke Leopold V of Austria in December 1192 and handed to Holy Roman Emperor Henry VI in March 1193. The agreed ransom was 150,000 marks of silver — roughly two to three times the Crown’s annual revenue.

The Ransom and Its Burden on England

The task of raising 150,000 marks fell on Hubert Walter and Eleanor of Aquitaine. Together they extracted the sum from across the Angevin Empire. The English contribution was punitive: a quarter tax on income and moveables (one of the most aggressive taxes of the medieval period); the entire wool clip of the Cistercian and Gilbertine monasteries; church plate seized from cathedrals; extraordinary tallages on the Jewish community recorded in the archae; a heavy scutage on tenants-in-chief who refused to serve in person; and special levies on towns and royal demesne. The first instalment was paid at Speyer in February 1194 and Richard was released. The remainder of the debt rumbled on for years.

The strain on England was severe. The Crown had already raised the Saladin Tithe in 1188 and squeezed the kingdom on Richard’s coronation in 1189. The 1193–94 ransom on top of that left the Treasury near empty. Inflation rose; baronial resentment hardened; the Cistercian monasteries protested at the loss of their wool clip. The taxes that John inherited — and his urgent need to keep extracting more — began here. Richard returned to England briefly in March 1194, was crowned a second time at Winchester to reaffirm his sovereignty, and crossed to Normandy in May 1194 to begin the war with Philip II that would consume the rest of his reign. He never came back. He was killed by a crossbow bolt at the siege of Châlus in Aquitaine on 6 April 1199.

The ransom shapes everything that follows. It financially exhausted England before John inherited the throne in 1199, leaving him a Treasury that needed continual replenishment. It hardened the use of scutage as a substitute for knight service, a practice John would push to breaking point. It set a precedent for taxing income and moveables that the Angevin Crown would return to in 1207. And it taught the barons that royal demands could escalate without limit, planting one of the seeds of the rebellion that ended at Runnymede.

Avoid restating the battles of Acre and Arsuf; the question asks why even those victories did not deliver Jerusalem. Use period vocabulary — Treaty of Jaffa, scutage, Latin kingdom — for top-band SPaG.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Richard could not recapture Jerusalem because of logistical limits, Philip II’s departure and threat to Normandy, internal Christian division, and Saladin’s patient scorched-earth strategy — the Treaty of Jaffa (September 1192) accepted Muslim control of the city in return for pilgrim access.
  • Returning home, Richard was wrecked in the Adriatic in December 1192, captured by Duke Leopold of Austria, and handed to Emperor Henry VI for a ransom of 150,000 marks of silver.
  • Hubert Walter and Eleanor of Aquitaine raised the ransom through a quarter tax, the Cistercian wool clip, church plate and extraordinary tallages — financially exhausting England and setting the pattern of escalating royal demands that John would inherit.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Treaty of Jaffa of September 1192.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for a valid identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Jerusalem retained by the Muslims — Saladin kept control of the Holy City, the central aim of the crusade not achieved.
• Coastal strip retained by the Christians — the Latin Kingdom kept Acre, Jaffa and a strip of coast as a base for any future crusade.
• Pilgrim access — unarmed Christian pilgrims were guaranteed safe passage to visit the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.
• Three-year truce — the agreement was set for an initial period of three years and eight months.
• Negotiated end to the campaign — the truce was concluded between Richard and Saladin without Philip II, who had already left, ending Richard’s share of the Third Crusade.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail; one may be more developed than the other.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or generic.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of how Richard’s ransom of 1193–94 was raised in England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Quarter tax on income and moveables — one of the most aggressive medieval taxes, levied at 25% of income and goods.
• Cistercian wool clip — the entire annual fleece of the Cistercian and Gilbertine monasteries was taken to fund the ransom.
• Church plate — gold and silver vessels were seized from cathedrals and monasteries to be melted down.
• Tallages on Jewish moneylenders — the archae were used to extract extraordinary sums from the Jewish community.
• Scutage on knight service — tenants-in-chief who would not serve in person paid heavy cash sums in lieu.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: Only one feature, or unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Richard I was captured on his journey home from the Holy Land.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Richard’s quarrel with Duke Leopold of Austria
• the closure of safer routes home
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Quarrel with Duke Leopold of Austria — Richard had thrown Leopold’s banner into the moat at Acre in 1191; Leopold sought a personal revenge that fed directly into Richard’s capture.
• Closure of safer routes — Philip II controlled the southern French coast and would have arrested him; Spanish coasts were closed by political agreements; Italy was unsafe because of the dispute with Henry VI.
• Forced choice of the Adriatic route — with western routes shut, Richard sailed north and tried to slip overland through the lands of his enemies.
• Storm and shipwreck — his ship was wrecked in the Adriatic in December 1192, leaving him to travel overland in disguise through hostile territory.
• Recognition near Vienna — the disguise failed; Richard was identified and seized in Erdberg near Vienna.
• Hostility of Henry VI — the Holy Roman Emperor was at odds with Richard over the rival Welf candidate Henry the Lion (Richard’s brother-in-law) and Sicily, and was happy to receive Richard from Leopold for ransom.
• Political vulnerability of an absentee crusader — Richard’s army had largely dispersed after the Treaty of Jaffa; he was travelling with a small retinue easy to ambush.
• Sheer profitability — the prospect of an enormous ransom from a king at war with France made Richard worth more alive than free.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence and clear weighting; both stimulus points developed; own information adds substance beyond the prompts.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation and supporting detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy; some narrative.
Emerging: Limited reasons; explanation thin or descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Richard I failed to recapture Jerusalem during the Third Crusade.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the supply lines from the coast
• the departure of Philip II
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explanation of distinct, supported reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• Supply lines — Jerusalem lay forty miles inland in arid hill country; even if captured, it would have had to be supplied by mule trains through Muslim-controlled territory after the western armies left.
• Philip II’s departure — the French king sailed home in August 1191, removing a substantial part of the army and unleashing political pressure on Richard’s lands in France.
• The threat from John and Philip — rumours that Richard’s brother and the French king were carving up the Angevin Empire forced him to plan an early return.
• Saladin’s scorched-earth strategy — he destroyed wells, cisterns and walls along the route to Jerusalem, denying water and shelter to the crusaders.
• Internal Christian division — the dispute between Conrad of Montferrat and Guy of Lusignan over the throne of Jerusalem split the high command; Pisans, Genoese, Templars and Hospitallers had rival agendas.
• The advice of the local barons of the Latin Kingdom — they argued any captured Jerusalem could not be held after the western army went home; Richard accepted their advice and turned back at Beit Nuba.

Mastering: Three or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Richard’s ransom of 1193–94 placed such a heavy burden on England.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the size of the ransom
• existing taxation since 1188
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• Sheer size — 150,000 marks of silver was equal to two or three years of total Crown revenue and had to be raised in months, not over a normal taxation cycle.
• Existing taxation — the Saladin Tithe of 1188 and the sale of offices at Richard’s coronation in 1189 had already drained reserves of cash and goodwill before the ransom was demanded.
• Aggressive levies — the quarter tax on income and moveables, the seizure of the Cistercian wool clip and church plate, the heavy scutage on tenants-in-chief, and tallages on the Jewish community fell on every part of society.
• Concentrated impact on the Church — whole monastic orders lost their main income source and cathedrals lost their plate, breeding lasting resentment.
• Damage to the wool trade — seizing the Cistercian fleece in one year disrupted England’s most valuable export trade.
• Lasting precedent — the ransom legitimised aggressive Crown taxation, a habit John inherited and pushed to breaking point.

Mastering: Three or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; both stimulus points developed and own information added.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Philip’s August 1191 departure removed a substantial fraction of the army.
• Once back in France, Philip plotted with John to seize Richard’s lands; the threat to Normandy created an unrelenting clock that drove Richard to compromise.
• Without Philip’s authority the joint legitimacy of the crusade was diminished, weakening Christian command at exactly the moment unified leadership was needed for an inland march on Jerusalem.
• The political pressure from France caused Richard to accept the Treaty of Jaffa in September 1192 rather than press on with another inland push.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Logistics — Jerusalem lay forty miles inland in waterless hill country; even Philip’s troops could not have solved the problem of supplying the city after capture.
• Saladin’s scorched-earth strategy — destruction of wells, cisterns and walls along the route denied the crusaders both water and bases.
• Internal Christian division — the Conrad of Montferrat / Guy of Lusignan dispute split the command; the Pisans, Genoese, Templars and Hospitallers all pulled in different directions.
• Advice of local barons — the Latin Kingdom barons told Richard a captured Jerusalem could not be held after the western armies left; their advice mattered as much as Philip’s absence.
• Length of campaign — the crusade had been on the road for over two years; supplies, horses and morale were running out regardless of French numbers.

Overall judgement: Philip’s departure created the political clock that forced compromise, but the strategic obstacles — logistics, Saladin’s denial of water, and the impossibility of holding a captured city — would have stopped the crusaders even if Philip had stayed. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly and reach a justified conclusion using precise period vocabulary (Beit Nuba, Treaty of Jaffa, Latin Kingdom, scutage).

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

lessons.title: John's Accession and the Murder of Prince Arthur
lessons.description: John’s contested claim, his rivalry with Arthur of Brittany, and his difficult character.
lessons.content_html:
When Richard I was killed by a crossbow bolt at the siege of Châlus on 6 April 1199, the Angevin Empire he left behind was vast but fragile. Two men could plausibly call themselves his heir. The first was Richard’s younger brother John, by then aged 32 and already master of Ireland and large estates in England. The second was a 12-year-old boy: Arthur of Brittany, the son of John’s elder dead brother Geoffrey. The choice between uncle and nephew would shape the next decade and end with one of the most controversial events of the reign.

John’s Claim to the Throne

John’s claim rested on a custom called proximity of blood: as the youngest surviving son of Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine, he was a direct adult heir. Arthur’s case rested on the rival rule of representation: a dead son’s line should inherit before his younger brothers. The Angevin lands split. England and Normandy accepted John, swayed by Eleanor of Aquitaine, William Marshal and Hubert Walter, who argued that the realm needed an adult king with a working knowledge of government. Anjou, Maine and Touraine declared for Arthur, who was already being raised by King Philip II of France — a deliberate move to keep him in French hands as a useful pawn.

John was crowned at Westminster on 27 May 1199. To secure Normandy he met Philip II at Le Goulet in May 1200 and signed a treaty: John was recognised as Richard’s heir on the Continent, but at the price of paying Philip a huge ‘relief’ (an inheritance fee) of 20,000 marks and ceding territory in the Vexin and Évreux. Contemporaries grumbled that John had bought what Richard had won, and gave him the unflattering nickname ‘John Softsword’.

Key Fact

John’s claim used proximity of blood (closest adult relative); Arthur of Brittany’s used representation (dead son’s line). England and Normandy accepted John; Anjou, Maine and Touraine declared for Arthur, who was sheltered by Philip II of France.

John’s Character

John was clever, energetic and far better at the daily grind of administration than his elder brother. The pipe rolls grew thicker every year of his reign as he toured England in person, hearing pleas, checking accounts and badgering sheriffs. But contemporaries also recorded a darker side. Roger of Wendover called him ‘cruel to all men’; the chronicler Matthew Paris — admittedly hostile — said hell itself was made fouler by his presence. Even allowing for monkish exaggeration, the pattern of distrust ran through everyone who dealt with him: he doubted the loyalty of his barons and they doubted the safety of their persons in his hands.

Three traits show up again and again. First, he was suspicious. He demanded hostages from his great barons — sons, wives and daughters held at court as a guarantee of good behaviour. Second, he was vindictive. The wife and son of William de Braose, his former close ally, were starved to death in Windsor Castle in 1210. Third, he was personally repellent in a way medieval kings were supposed not to be: he flirted with the wives and daughters of his barons, made bad jokes at their expense, and lacked the easy comradeship of Richard. None of this would have mattered if he had been winning. Once he started losing, it mattered very much.

Students often arrive thinking ‘bad King John’ is a settled fact. Modern historians, especially W.L. Warren, have stressed his administrative competence: detailed pipe-roll record-keeping, energetic itinerant justice, careful taxation experiments. He inherited a financially exhausted kingdom from Richard’s crusade and ransom and squeezed every shilling out of it. The problem was not that he was lazy or stupid — he was neither — but that his methods of squeezing revenue were too efficient and too arbitrary, and that his personal style alienated almost everyone he needed to lead.

The Rivalry with Arthur of Brittany

Arthur grew up in the French court and, as a teenager, became a useful weapon for Philip II. In 1202 Philip used the appeal of the disgruntled Lusignan family — whose head, Hugh, had been betrothed to Isabella of Angoulême before John snatched her away as his queen — to summon John to Paris as Duke of Aquitaine. When John refused to attend, Philip declared his French fiefs forfeit and gave Anjou and Brittany to Arthur. The 15-year-old now led a military campaign against his own grandmother, Eleanor of Aquitaine, besieging her at Mirebeau Castle in Poitou in late July 1202.

John’s response was the most decisive military action of his reign. He marched 130 km in 48 hours, surprised the besiegers at dawn on 1 August 1202, and captured Arthur, the leading Lusignans, and around 250 Poitevin knights. It was a stunning victory and could have stabilised his French position for a generation.

The Murder of Arthur

Arthur was imprisoned first at Falaise and then at Rouen. After early 1203 he was never seen alive again. The most credible contemporary account — the Margam Annals — reports that on 3 April 1203 a drunken John personally killed his nephew, weighted the body with a stone and threw it into the Seine. Other versions have Arthur murdered on John’s orders or dying after a botched attempt to blind and castrate him. Either way, the responsibility fell on the king. The political consequences were immediate and catastrophic: Norman, Breton and Poitevin barons who had previously kept their distance from Philip II now switched sides. The Bretons took Arthur’s death as a personal blood feud against John. The atrocity dissolved the loyalty that John needed to defend Normandy in the year that followed.

Key Fact

John captured Arthur of Brittany at Mirebeau on 1 August 1202 in a brilliant lightning march. Arthur was murdered at Rouen, probably on 3 April 1203. The killing destroyed John’s standing among his French vassals and prepared the ground for the loss of Normandy a year later.

Medieval politics ran on personal trust. A king who would imprison and probably murder his own nephew — a captured noble protected by the customs of noble captivity — could not be trusted to keep his word with anyone else. The Bretons rose; the leading Poitevin barons reopened negotiations with Philip; rumours spread that John had personally done the deed. When Philip’s forces invaded Normandy in 1203 they met a duchy whose nobility had already decided the king did not deserve their loyalty.

By the spring of 1203, John had crowned himself, bought a peace with Philip, won a brilliant battle at Mirebeau, and then thrown the goodwill away. He had inherited the most successful royal house in Europe and, within four years of accession, had set in motion the chain of events that would lose Normandy and his French inheritance forever. The next lesson examines exactly how that loss unfolded.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark Describe Two Features question on John’s character, choose two genuinely distinct features — for example, his administrative energy (touring England in person, thickening pipe rolls) and his vindictiveness (the starvation of the de Braose family in 1210, the murder of Arthur). Avoid restating the same trait twice. Each feature needs one supporting detail (a name, a date, a place) and the two features must be separated as distinct points, not blurred into one paragraph.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • John’s claim to the throne in 1199 used proximity of blood; Arthur of Brittany’s used representation. England and Normandy accepted John; Anjou, Maine and Touraine declared for Arthur, sheltered by Philip II.
  • John’s character combined real administrative ability with suspicion, vindictiveness and a personal style that alienated his barons; the ‘cartoon villain’ image is exaggerated but the distrust was real.
  • John captured Arthur at Mirebeau on 1 August 1202 but was almost certainly responsible for his murder at Rouen in April 1203; the killing fatally damaged his standing among his French vassals and set up the loss of Normandy.

practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks. Two distinct features must be given.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Administrative energy — John toured England in person, hearing pleas and checking accounts; the pipe rolls grew thicker every year of his reign.
• Suspicion of his barons — he demanded hostages, including the sons and wives of leading nobles, as a guarantee of good behaviour.
• Vindictiveness — he starved Matilda de Braose and her son to death at Windsor in 1210.
• Cleverness combined with arbitrariness — he experimented with new taxes (the 1207 thirteenth) and creative justice but applied them inconsistently.
• Personal repulsiveness to chroniclers — Roger of Wendover called him ‘cruel to all men’; Matthew Paris said hell was made fouler by his presence.
• Lack of military reputation — the nickname ‘Softsword’ followed his peace at Le Goulet.

• Eleanor of Aquitaine’s backing — the queen-mother used her authority to swing England, Normandy and her own duchy of Aquitaine behind John.
• Coronation at Westminster — John was anointed and crowned by the Archbishop of Canterbury on 27 May 1199, broadcasting legitimacy.
• Treaty of Le Goulet (May 1200) — Philip II of France formally recognised John as Richard’s heir on the Continent in return for a 20,000-mark relief and territorial concessions.

Indicative content:
• Breach of noble captivity — medieval custom held that captured nobles were ransomed or honourably imprisoned, never killed; John’s probable murder of his own nephew at Rouen in 1203 broke that code openly.
• Breton blood feud — Arthur was the natural lord of Brittany; his murder turned the duchy from a wavering territory into a sworn enemy of John, opening Normandy’s western flank to attack.

• Loss of moral authority — chroniclers spread the story across Europe, blackening John’s reputation at the very moment he needed allies.
• Philip II’s legal cover — Philip used the murder to maintain that John was an unworthy vassal whose fiefs could justly be confiscated.
• Symbolic loss — capturing Arthur at Mirebeau in August 1202 had been John’s greatest victory; throwing away that goodwill made the murder politically as well as morally a disaster.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• The murder of Arthur in 1203 broke the customs of noble captivity and turned Brittany into a blood feud against the king.
• The starvation of the de Braose family at Windsor in 1210 was the most extreme example of a wider pattern of vindictiveness that frightened all great barons.
• John’s habit of demanding hostages from leading nobles and flirting with their wives and daughters destroyed personal trust.
• Chroniclers from Roger of Wendover to Matthew Paris record near-universal disgust with his personal manner.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Philip II of France was a determined and skilful enemy; he had been working to break up the Angevin Empire since the 1180s and would have looked for any pretext.
• Structural Angevin weakness — the empire stretched from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees, was held together only by personal loyalty, and was financially exhausted by Richard’s ransom.
• The Lusignan affair — John’s seizure of Isabella of Angoulême from her Lusignan betrothed gave Philip a legitimate legal pretext to summon and condemn John.
• The fall of Château Gaillard in March 1204 was a question of military and engineering circumstances as much as character.
• Loss of revenue — even a popular king would have struggled to defend Normandy without the Angevin treasury Richard had drained.

Overall judgement: John’s personal character was the spark, but only because his strategic position was already vulnerable. Philip II would have moved in any case; structural Angevin weaknesses made any war hard to win; but the murder of Arthur and the king’s general untrustworthiness turned a difficult position into a hopeless one. A balanced judgement weighs character as the trigger against structural and external factors as the underlying conditions.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout (proximity of blood, representation, relief, Lusignan, Mirebeau).
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.
